title: Melanopsin Cells: Light for the Clock and the Pupil

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: What makes a retinal ganglion cell an intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cell (ipRGC)?
cards.back: It makes its own light response using melanopsin and also relays rod and cone signals received through bipolar cells.
cards.quote: a ganglion cell that makes its own light response with the pigment melanopsin and also relays signals that rods and cones send through bipolar cells.

cards.front: Alignment of the circadian clock with day and night by light is called {{c1::photoentrainment}}.
cards.quote: Light reaching the SCN shifts the clock so that it stays aligned with day and night.

cards.front: Which brain targets of ipRGCs serve the circadian clock and the pupil light reflex?
cards.back: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) serves the clock; the olivary pretectal nucleus (OPN) drives the pupil light reflex.
cards.quote: The olivary pretectal nucleus (OPN) drives the pupil light reflex.

cards.front: A retinal ganglion cell still depolarizes to light after synaptic transmission from photoreceptors is verifiably blocked. What does this show?
cards.back: The cell has an intrinsic light response; the remaining response does not require the rod and cone synaptic relay.
cards.quote: If a ganglion cell still responds to light once that block is verified, the response is its own.
cards.section: A light response that survives the block

cards.front: A retinal ganglion cell responds to light after a synaptic blocker is added, but the block was not verified. If transmission remains partly intact, could the response persist without intrinsic photosensitivity, and why?
cards.back: Yes. Residual rod and cone transmission could still drive the cell. Verify the synaptic block before attributing a surviving light response to intrinsic photosensitivity.
cards.quote: If a ganglion cell still responds to light once that block is verified, the response is its own.
cards.section: A light response that survives the block

cards.front: How does the typical melanopsin response of an ipRGC differ from its relayed rod and cone response under the same light?
cards.back: It is slower, less sensitive and slower to decay after light-off. Both inputs can sustain responses; the differences depend on subtype and illumination.
cards.quote: One is the usually faster, more sensitive signal that rods and cones send through bipolar cells. The other is its own typically slower, less sensitive melanopsin response.
cards.section: The signature response

cards.front: Why is a slow, sustained ipRGC light response useful for the clock and pupil?
cards.back: These outputs need a steady measure of brightness over time rather than rapid information about edges.
cards.quote: The clock and the pupil need to know how bright it is, and how bright it has stayed, not where the edges are.
cards.section: The signature response

cards.front: In humans, the pupil remaining small after light-off is the {{c1::post-illumination pupil response}}.
cards.back: The slow decay of the intrinsic ipRGC response supports this persistence.
cards.quote: the post-illumination pupil response, in which the pupil stays small for a while after a light goes off;
cards.section: The signature response

cards.front: Through which retinal cell type do rods and cones send signals to ipRGC dendrites?
cards.back: Bipolar cells.
cards.quote: Rods and cones signal to bipolar cells, and bipolar cells signal to the ipRGC's dendrites.
cards.section: Two inputs, one exit: how light becomes a voltage

cards.front: Why does light-induced closure of cation channels hyperpolarize a rod?
cards.back: Less positive charge enters the rod, so its membrane becomes more negative.
cards.quote: Light closes cation channels in a rod, through the cGMP cascade in senses and cGMP, so less positive charge enters and the rod hyperpolarizes.
cards.section: Two inputs, one exit: how light becomes a voltage

cards.front: What is the intrinsic phototransduction pathway described for mouse M1 ipRGCs, including the uncertainty about the G protein?
cards.back: Melanopsin → G protein, probably of the Gq family (inferred) → PLCB4 → opening of TRPC6 and TRPC7 channels.
cards.quote: a G protein, probably of the Gq family (inferred; Xue and colleagues did not identify the G-alpha), phospholipase C beta 4 (PLCB4)
cards.section: Two inputs, one exit: how light becomes a voltage

cards.front: A neuron rests at a negative voltage dominated by potassium conductance. Nonselective cation channels with a reversal potential near 0 mV open. What happens to voltage and why?
cards.back: It depolarizes toward 0 mV, because the added conductance gives that reversal potential more weight in the conductance-weighted balance point.
cards.quote: Opening channels gives more weight to their reversal potential, so the balance point moves up from near E_K toward 0 mV, and the cell depolarizes.
cards.section: Two inputs, one exit: how light becomes a voltage

cards.front: In an illustrative passive model, E_K = −90 mV and E_cation = 0 mV. Conductances are in common arbitrary units. With g_K = 1, raise g_cation from 0.2 to 1. Using V = Σ(gE)/Σg, find both voltages and the change.
cards.back: Initially V = [1(−90) + 0.2(0)]/1.2 = −75 mV. Finally V = [1(−90) + 1(0)]/2 = −45 mV. The change is +30 mV: depolarization. These are model values, not ipRGC measurements.
cards.quote: With illustrative values in a passive model (not ipRGC measurements), a potassium conductance of 1 and a cation conductance of 0.2,
cards.section: Two inputs, one exit: how light becomes a voltage

cards.front: A neuron sits above E_K. Potassium leak conductance falls while a depolarizing cation conductance stays open. What happens to voltage and why?
cards.back: It depolarizes: reducing potassium conductance reduces the weight pulling the balance point toward E_K.
cards.quote: closing potassium channels in a cell sitting above E_K also depolarizes it, by the same rule.
cards.section: Two inputs, one exit: how light becomes a voltage

cards.front: Acute suppression of a nocturnal mouse’s running by bright light at night, independently of a clock shift, is called {{c1::masking}}.
cards.quote: A third readout is masking: bright light at night commonly suppresses a nocturnal mouse's running acutely, independently of any clock shift.
cards.section: Remove the pigment, or remove the cell

cards.front: A mouse starts running at the same time relative to lights-off each day. Design a follow-up to distinguish clock entrainment from acute masking by light.
cards.back: Release it into constant darkness and examine where the running rhythm begins. The rule is that masking can mimic locking to a light cycle; removing the light reveals where the clock itself was set.
cards.quote: Because masking can make running look locked to the cycle, releasing the mouse into constant darkness shows where the clock itself was set.
cards.section: Remove the pigment, or remove the cell

cards.front: Why can a mouse lacking melanopsin still entrain to a light-dark cycle?
cards.back: Its ipRGCs remain and can relay rod and cone input to the clock. Removing the pigment removes only one input.
cards.quote: Either input alone is enough for the clock to entrain and for the pupil to constrict.
cards.section: Remove the pigment, or remove the cell

cards.front: In a mouse without functional rods or cones but with melanopsin intact, predict the pupil response to sustained bright light and explain it.
cards.back: Constriction is slower and less sensitive, but sustained and can reach its normal maximum in bright light. The fast, sensitive rod and cone drive is lost, while melanopsin can hold constriction.
cards.quote: The rod and cone signals make constriction quick and sensitive, especially in dim light and at the start of a light,
cards.section: Remove the pigment, or remove the cell

cards.front: Mouse ipRGC ablation causes larger clock and pupil deficits than melanopsin deletion, despite intact rods and cones. What routing conclusion does this support?
cards.back: ipRGCs are the main route to the clock and pupil for both intrinsic melanopsin signals and relayed rod and cone signals.
cards.quote: So in mice the ipRGCs are the main route by which rod, cone and melanopsin signals reach the clock and the pupil.
cards.section: Remove the pigment, or remove the cell

cards.front: Why does a small residual pupil response after progressive, incomplete mouse ipRGC ablation fail to prove a separate bypass route?
cards.back: Surviving ipRGCs could carry the residual response. The result permits a weak bypass but does not establish one.
cards.quote: kills the cells progressively and incompletely, with more lost as the mice age, and some pupil response remained, so a weak bypass cannot be excluded.
cards.section: Remove the pigment, or remove the cell

cards.front: A hypothetical clock receives inputs A and B. A light pulse shifts it 2.0 h with both inputs, 0.6 h with B alone, 1.8 h with A alone and 0.0 h with neither. Calculate the summed single-input losses and compare with the loss of both.
cards.back: Loss of A: 2.0 − 0.6 = 1.4 h. Loss of B: 2.0 − 1.8 = 0.2 h. Sum: 1.6 h. Losing both costs 2.0 − 0.0 = 2.0 h. The losses are not additive.
cards.quote: A single knockout shows what the other input can do alone, not each input's share.
cards.section: Remove the pigment, or remove the cell

cards.front: In a hypothetical clock pathway, either sensory input alone produces a phase shift, but their isolated shifts sum to more than the shift with both inputs. Does this locate saturation within the sensory cell?
cards.back: No. A ceiling on pooled output is one possible explanation, but it could arise in the sensory cell or downstream. The rule is that nonadditive losses do not assign fixed input shares or identify where the nonlinearity occurs.
cards.quote: These numbers do not say where the saturation happens, in the cell or downstream, and other explanations are possible.
cards.section: Remove the pigment, or remove the cell

cards.front: After Brn3b-positive ipRGCs are ablated in mice, pupil constriction is severely impaired but photoentrainment survives. Interpret the spared clock response.
cards.back: Brn3b-negative SCN-projecting cells remain. The two behaviours depend on partly different output sets; surviving entrainment does not show that ipRGCs are dispensable.
cards.quote: Genetic ablation of the Brn3b-positive cells severely impaired the pupil light reflex and spared circadian photoentrainment, because the Brn3b-negative cells that reach the SCN remained.
cards.section: Separate cells for the clock and the pupil

cards.front: Why does the Brn3b-positive ipRGC ablation not assign the pupil reflex to one mouse subtype?
cards.back: Brn3b-positive ipRGCs comprise a mixed set of more than one type; the marker defines an output set rather than a single subtype.
cards.quote: Because Brn3b marks a mixed output set, the result separates two behaviours without assigning either to one subtype.
cards.section: Separate cells for the clock and the pupil

cards.front: Where do mouse M2 and M3 ipRGC dendrites lie within the two bands of the inner plexiform layer?
cards.back: M2 dendrites occupy the inner band; M3 dendrites occupy both bands.
cards.quote: ipRGC dendrites gather in two bands of that layer, an outer one and an inner one.
cards.section: Separate cells for the clock and the pupil

cards.front: Which familiar mouse retinal ganglion cell type is the M4 ipRGC?
cards.back: The sustained ON alpha ganglion cell.
cards.quote: M4 was recorded as intrinsically photosensitive by Ecker and colleagues in 2010, linked to ON alpha cells by Estevez and colleagues in 2012,
cards.section: Subtype counts and how each was assigned

cards.front: Mouse M5 and M6 ipRGC axons reach the dLGN, a thalamic relay for image-forming vision. What role would you investigate, and does that projection alone demonstrate it?
cards.back: Investigate contributions to pattern vision. A projection motivates a functional hypothesis but does not establish subtype-specific behaviour; M6-specific behaviour was not tested in the cited tracing work.
cards.quote: The M5 and M6 projections to the dLGN are one reason to ask whether ipRGCs also help with seeing patterns,
cards.section: Separate cells for the clock and the pupil

cards.front: The mouse light schedule with alternating 3.5-hour light and 3.5-hour dark intervals is called the {{c1::T7 cycle}}.
cards.quote: a T7 cycle, 3.5 hours of light followed by 3.5 hours of dark,
cards.section: Beyond the clock: light, mood and learning in mice

cards.front: T7 mice showed depression-like behaviour with preserved total sleep and a still-rhythmic clock whose period lengthened. What simple explanations do these controls challenge?
cards.back: Simple sleep loss or complete loss of circadian rhythmicity. They do not establish normal circadian timing or diagnose human depression.
cards.quote: The authors cite earlier work showing that total sleep and sleep architecture are preserved under T7, and they found the clock still rhythmic,
cards.section: Beyond the clock: light, mood and learning in mice

cards.front: In a hypothetical pathway, ablating a light-sensitive relay neuron removes a behavioural response. The neuron both detects light itself and relays other photoreceptors. Design a test of which input matters.
cards.back: Compare selective loss of its pigment with selective loss of upstream photoreceptor signalling, while retaining the neuron and measuring the same response. The rule is that cell ablation removes both inputs, so ablation alone cannot distinguish their contributions.
cards.quote: An ablation shows that the cells are needed, but because it removes both inputs it cannot say whether the melanopsin response or the rod and cone relay
cards.section: Remove the pigment, or remove the cell

cards.front: In the tested mouse paradigms, PHb silencing prevented the mood-like change and PHb activation produced one. What causal claims do these interventions support?
cards.back: PHb activity was needed for the tested mood-like change, and its activation was sufficient to produce one in those paradigms. This does not demonstrate a homologous human circuit.
cards.quote: In the tested paradigms, silencing PHb prevented the mood-like change, and activating it was enough to produce one.
cards.section: Beyond the clock: light, mood and learning in mice

cards.front: Why should T7 learning deficits in mice retaining mainly SCN-projecting ipRGCs not be assigned exclusively to SCN innervation?
cards.back: Minor non-SCN innervation remained, and its contribution was not excluded.
cards.quote: although minor non-SCN innervation remained in this model and its contribution was not excluded.
cards.section: Beyond the clock: light, mood and learning in mice

cards.front: A report claims one blind participant without functional rods or cones showed a pupil action spectrum, above-chance light detection and melatonin suppression. What is wrong with combining the Zaidi study results this way?
cards.back: The pupil action spectrum and forced-choice light detection came from the woman; melatonin suppression came from the man. They were two different participants, not one combined demonstration.
cards.quote: The two results come from two different people and must not be merged.
cards.section: What people show: two blind participants and an evening screen

cards.front: What do the two profoundly blind participants without functional rods or cones establish about human photoreception?
cards.back: An existence proof of inner-retinal contributions to pupil responses and melatonin suppression, not a population estimate, restored image vision or an ipRGC necessity test.
cards.quote: Together they are an existence proof that human inner-retinal photoreception can drive a pupil response and melatonin suppression, not a population result,
cards.section: What people show: two blind participants and an evening screen

cards.front: An experiment compares a bright light-emitting device with a printed book and finds delayed melatonin onset. Design a follow-up to distinguish spectral effects from brightness effects.
cards.back: Vary spectrum at matched brightness, and brightness with spectrum held fixed. The rule is that changing both together confounds their effects. Even a separated light effect would not directly establish which retinal cells are necessary.
cards.quote: The study did not manipulate ipRGCs and did not separate the device light's spectrum from its brightness,
cards.section: What people show: two blind participants and an evening screen

cards.front: Why compare a striped grating with a grey field of the same average luminance when testing vision in mice lacking rod and cone signalling?
cards.back: Matching mean luminance prevents overall brightness from being the distinguishing cue. Successful discrimination supports coarse pattern vision, not normal acuity.
cards.quote: Mice lacking rod and cone signalling (Gnat1 and Cnga3 knockouts) discriminated a striped grating from a grey field of the same average luminance.
cards.section: A smaller extension: coarse patterns and contrast

cards.front: Design pupil measurements that distinguish loss of fast rod/cone drive from loss of sustained melanopsin drive in mice.
cards.back: Measure rapid constriction in dim light and maintenance over minutes in steady bright light. The rule is that rods and cones make the reflex quick and sensitive, whereas melanopsin holds bright-light constriction; an endpoint alone can miss the difference.
cards.quote: For the pupil, measure constriction over minutes in steady bright light, where melanopsin holds the response, and quick responses in dim light, where rods and cones dominate.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why does detecting a photopigment’s messenger RNA in a retinal cell fail to establish that the cell responds to light?
cards.back: It shows gene expression, not a functional light response. A transcript alone does not establish photosensitivity.
cards.quote: It located a gene's expression and recorded no light response; a transcript alone does not make a cell light-sensitive.
cards.section: Four discoveries, four dates

cards.front: A developmental neuronal ablation changes an adult light-driven response. What alternative explanation would an adult-timed ablation help address?
cards.back: Developmental rewiring could contribute to the adult phenotype. Killing the cells only in adulthood avoids developmental rewiring as an explanation for the response change.
cards.quote: That design avoids developmental rewiring as an explanation.
cards.section: An ablation timed in adults

cards.front: How can mouse M1 ipRGC dendrites lie in the OFF stratum yet receive ON bipolar input?
cards.back: OFF names the dendritic position. Some ON bipolar axons form ribbon synapses in passing through that layer, including onto M1 dendrites.
cards.quote: M1 dendrites sit in the OFF stratum, yet M1 cells receive ON bipolar input.
cards.section: Subtype counts and how each was assigned

cards.front: Is an HCN contribution to mouse M2 and M4 ipRGC phototransduction established across laboratories?
cards.back: No. It remains disputed; recording conditions may contribute to the disagreement.
cards.quote: Whether HCN channels contribute in M2 and M4 cells is an open disagreement between laboratories
cards.section: Channels beyond M1: an open disagreement

cards.front: A representative mouse M4 cell is voltage-clamped with synaptic transmission blocked. Holding current is +31.28 pA in darkness and −27.48 pA in light. With outward positive, calculate light minus dark and interpret its direction.
cards.back: ΔI = (−27.48) − (+31.28) = −58.76 pA: an inward shift with outward positive. This is a current change in one cell, not a group average or a measured depolarization.
cards.quote: The holding current at a fixed voltage was +31.28 pA in the dark and -27.48 pA in light.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a photocurrent

cards.front: A neuron held at fixed voltage shows an inward current shift during light, with outward positive. Can the trace alone distinguish cation-channel opening from potassium-channel closure or demonstrate depolarization?
cards.back: No. More inward cation current and less outward potassium current can both give an inward shift. The rules are that net-current changes do not identify a channel and voltage clamp holds voltage fixed. Either change could depolarize an unclamped cell.
cards.quote: An inward shift can mean more inward current (cation channels opening) or less outward current (potassium channels closing), and the subtraction cannot tell them apart,
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a photocurrent

cards.front: Verified HCN blockade leaves the mouse M4 photocurrent unreduced in the short-incubation preparation. Four cells also show no significant light-induced HCN tail-current change. How far does this evidence go?
cards.back: It argues that HCN opening is not necessary for the response in this preparation. The rules are that a verified blockade tests necessity under its conditions, and a nonsignificant difference does not prove equality. It does not settle the interlaboratory dispute.
cards.quote: That argues against HCN opening being necessary for the M4 response in this preparation.
cards.section: Worked problem: reading a photocurrent
